passages.title: The Footprint in the Sand
passages.text:
It happened one day, about noon, going towards my boat, I was exceedingly surprised with the print of a man's naked foot on the shore, which was very plain to be seen on the sand. I stood like one thunderstruck, or as if I had seen an apparition. I listened, I looked round me, but I could hear nothing, nor see anything; I went up to a rising ground to look farther; I went up the shore and down the shore, but it was all one; I could see no other impression but that one. I went to it again to see if there were any more, and to observe if it might not be my fancy; but there was no room for that, for there was exactly the print of a foot--toes, heel, and every part of a foot. How it came thither I knew not, nor could I in the least imagine; but after innumerable fluttering thoughts, like a man perfectly confused and out of myself, I came home to my fortification, not feeling, as we say, the ground I went on, but terrified to the last degree, looking behind me at every two or three steps, mistaking every bush and tree, and fancying every stump at a distance to be a man. Nor is it possible to describe how many various shapes my affrighted imagination represented things to me in, how many wild ideas were found every moment in my fancy, and what strange, unaccountable whimsies came into my thoughts by the way.

When I came to my castle (for so I think I called it ever after this), I fled into it like one pursued. Whether I went over by the ladder, as first contrived, or went in at the hole in the rock, which I had called a door, I cannot remember; no, nor could I remember the next morning, for never frightened hare fled to cover, or fox to earth, with more terror of mind than I to this retreat.

I slept none that night; the farther I was from the occasion of my fright, the greater my apprehensions were, which is something contrary to the nature of such things, and especially to the usual practice of all creatures in fear; but I was so embarrassed with my own frightful ideas of the thing, that I formed nothing but dismal imaginations to myself, even though I was now a great way off. Sometimes I fancied it must be the devil, and reason joined in with me in this supposition, for how should any other thing in human shape come into the place? Where was the vessel that brought them? What marks were there of any other footstep? And how was it possible a man should come there? But then, to think that Satan should take human shape upon him in such a place, where there could be no manner of occasion for it, but to leave the print of his foot behind him, and that even for no purpose too, for he could not be sure I should see it--this was an amusement the other way. I considered that the devil might have found out abundance of other ways to have terrified me than this of the single print of a foot; that as I lived quite on the other side of the island, he would never have been so simple as to leave a mark in a place where it was ten thousand to one whether I should ever see it or not, and in the sand too, which the first surge of the sea, upon a high wind, would have defaced entirely. All this seemed inconsistent with the thing itself and with all the notions we usually entertain of the subtlety of the devil.
passages.source_note: Public domain: from Robinson Crusoe by Daniel Defoe (1719). Straight quotation marks substituted for typographic ones.

questions.stem: At what time of day does the narrator make his discovery?

options.text: At dawn
About noon
In the late evening
At midnight
Just before sunset

questions.explanation: The opening line places the event 'about noon'.

questions.stem: Where was the narrator heading when he was startled?

options.text: Towards his castle
Up a rising ground
Down to the vessel
Towards his boat
Along the far side of the island

questions.explanation: He was 'going towards my boat' when he saw the mark.

questions.stem: According to the narrator, what could destroy a mark left in the sand?

options.text: The heat of the noon sun
The tramping of wild creatures
A heavy fall of rain
The passing of another man
The first surge of the sea in a high wind

questions.explanation: He notes the sea 'upon a high wind, would have defaced entirely' such a mark.

questions.stem: What does the narrator's reaction suggest he had believed about the island until this moment?

options.text: That it was regularly visited by traders
That wild animals were his chief danger
That he was its only human inhabitant
That a rescue ship would soon arrive
That the sand never held any marks

questions.explanation: His terror at a single human footprint only makes sense if he had thought himself entirely alone.

questions.stem: In this passage, 'thunderstruck' most nearly describes someone who is

options.text: stunned and unable to move
burned by lightning
deafened by a loud noise
furiously angry
soaked by a sudden storm

questions.explanation: He stands 'like one thunderstruck', frozen as though he had seen a ghost.

questions.stem: 'Or as if I had seen an apparition' is an example of which device?

options.text: Metaphor
Simile
Onomatopoeia
Alliteration
Hyperbole

questions.explanation: The comparison is made with 'as if', which marks it as a simile.

questions.stem: What does going 'up the shore and down the shore' reveal about the narrator?

options.text: He is trying to escape as fast as he can
He enjoys a leisurely walk along the beach
He is looking for his lost boat
He has already forgotten the print
He searches thoroughly, needing to be certain of what he has seen

questions.explanation: Pacing the beach in both directions shows him checking carefully for other marks.

questions.stem: Why does the author list 'toes, heel, and every part of a foot'?

options.text: To show the narrator admires the shape of feet
To suggest the foot belonged to a giant
To prove the print was real and not imagined
To hint that the print was very old
To describe the narrator's own footprints

questions.explanation: The precise anatomy removes any 'room' for the mark to be mere fancy.

questions.stem: When the narrator says he came home 'not feeling, as we say, the ground I went on', he means that he

options.text: had lost all feeling in his legs from injury
was too shaken to notice how he walked
walked on soft ground that made no sound
floated above the sand like a spirit
could not decide which path to take

questions.explanation: The phrase conveys distraction and shock, not literal numbness.

questions.stem: What is the effect of describing 'every stump at a distance to be a man'?

options.text: It proves men really were hiding on the island
It suggests the island is crowded with people
It shows how terror makes him misread harmless things as threats
It shows his eyesight is failing
It reveals his affection for the landscape

questions.explanation: A terrified mind turns ordinary stumps into imagined men, dramatising his panic.

questions.stem: The word 'whimsies' carries a sense of ideas that are

options.text: carefully reasoned conclusions
cheerful and comforting daydreams
practical plans for escape
solemn religious beliefs
odd and fleeting fancies

questions.explanation: Paired with 'strange, unaccountable', it means passing, irrational notions.

questions.stem: Which of these happens immediately after the narrator first sees the mark?

options.text: He climbs the ladder into his castle
He lies awake through the night
He stands still, as if he had seen a ghost
He decides it must be the devil
He measures the print with his hands

questions.explanation: The very next sentence has him standing frozen like one thunderstruck.

questions.stem: Which quotation best shows that the narrator's fear grew stronger the safer he became?

options.text: 'the farther I was from the occasion of my fright, the greater my apprehensions were'
'I could see no other impression but that one'
'I fled into it like one pursued'
'How it came thither I knew not'
'I listened, I looked round me'

questions.explanation: This line directly states the paradox that distance increased, rather than eased, his dread.

questions.stem: Which phrase compares the narrator to a hunted animal?

options.text: 'I formed nothing but dismal imaginations'
'never frightened hare fled to cover, or fox to earth'
'this was an amusement the other way'
'terrified to the last degree'
'a great way off'

questions.explanation: He likens his flight to a hare running to cover and a fox to its earth.

questions.stem: The tone of the passage is best described as

options.text: calm and detached
cheerful and hopeful
bitter and resentful
playful and teasing
anxious and fearful

questions.explanation: The vocabulary of terror, dread and dismal imaginings gives an anxious, fearful tone.

questions.stem: By what two ways might the narrator have entered his stronghold?

options.text: By the boat or across the shore
Over the wall or under a gate
Through a door in the sand or a tunnel
Down the rising ground or up a tree
By the ladder or through the hole in the rock

questions.explanation: He recalls he either 'went over by the ladder' or 'went in at the hole in the rock'.

questions.stem: Why does the narrator finally reject the idea that the devil left the print?

options.text: It would be too pointless and unlikely a thing for so cunning a being to do
He has proof the devil cannot walk on sand
A priest had told him devils leave no marks
He saw the true owner of the foot
The print was far too large for any devil

questions.explanation: He reasons the devil would not 'be so simple' as to leave a mark to no purpose in so unlikely a spot.

questions.stem: Why does the writer fill the final part of the passage with a string of questions such as 'Where was the vessel that brought them?'

options.text: To dramatise the narrator's restless attempt to reason out the mystery
To show he already knows all the answers
To address the reader for advice
To pass the time until morning
To mock the idea that anyone else exists

questions.explanation: The piled-up questions mirror a mind turning the puzzle over and over without rest.

questions.stem: The second paragraph, beginning 'When I came to my castle', mainly serves to do what?

options.text: To explain how the shelter was first built
To introduce a new character on the island
To return the narrator calmly to his daily work
To describe his panicked retreat into his shelter
To describe the sea defacing the sand

questions.explanation: The paragraph carries him from the shore into his 'castle' in a state of flight.

questions.stem: Which conclusion about the narrator's home is best supported by the passage?

options.text: It sits directly beside the boat
It floats offshore on the vessel
It stands on the open, unprotected sand
It lies far from the beach where the print was found
It can be seen from the rising ground at once

questions.explanation: He says he 'lived quite on the other side of the island', so his home is remote from the shore mark.

questions.stem: As it is used here, the word 'defaced' is closest in meaning to

options.text: painted over
carved deeper
wiped away
made larger
left untouched

questions.explanation: The surging sea would rub the mark out of the sand entirely.

questions.stem: How much sleep does the narrator get on the night after his fright?

options.text: None at all
A short, uneasy nap
A full and restful night
He sleeps only at dawn
He sleeps deeply from exhaustion

questions.explanation: He states plainly, 'I slept none that night'.

questions.stem: Why does the narrator mention that 'reason joined in with me in this supposition'?

options.text: To prove that his fears were entirely unreasonable
To introduce a friend named Reason
To show he had stopped thinking altogether
To show that even his logical mind, for a moment, agreed with his dread
To argue that the print was harmless

questions.explanation: The remark lends weight to his dread by suggesting reason briefly agreed with it.

questions.stem: In 'my affrighted imagination represented things to me', what part of speech is 'affrighted'?

options.text: Verb
Adverb
Noun
Adjective
Preposition

questions.explanation: 'Affrighted' describes the noun 'imagination', so it acts as an adjective here.

questions.stem: Which best describes the overall movement of the passage?

options.text: From calm reflection to a happy discovery
From a sudden shock, through flight, to troubled reasoning
From a long journey to a safe arrival home
From an argument to a peaceful agreement
From boredom to sudden excitement and joy

questions.explanation: It opens with the shock of the print, moves to his frightened retreat, and ends with him reasoning over its cause.
